title: Ovid, Caesar, and Poetic Apotheosis
subtitle: A poem's account of Caesar becoming a star

learningObjectives.text: What does Venus ask the gods to prevent?
How does Ovid's poem describe Caesar's soul after his death?

plea.author: Ovid
plea.locator: Book XV · Fable VIII [XV.745-879]; Book XV · Fable VIII [XV.745-879], normalized characters 1373-2278
plea.excerpt: Behold, on how vast a scale treason is plotted against me, and with how great perfidy that life is sought, which alone remains for me from the Dardanian Iülus. Shall I alone be everlastingly harassed by justified anxieties? I, whom one while the Calydonian lance of the son of Tydeus is wounding, {and} at another time the walls of Troy, defended in vain, are grieving? I, who have seen my son driven about in protracted wanderings, tossed on the ocean, entering the abodes of the departed, and waging war with Turnus; or, if we confess the truth, with Juno rather? {But}, why am I now calling to mind the ancient misfortunes of my own offspring? Present apprehensions do not allow me to remember things of former days. Against me, you behold how the impious swords are {now} being whetted. Avert them, I entreat; hinder this crime, and do not, by the murder of the priest, extinguish the flames of Vesta.
plea.note: Verbatim translated verse from Ovid. Riley's arguments, synopses, notes, and explanations are separately indexed and are not quoted as primary verse.

star.author: Ovid
star.locator: Book XV · Fable VIII [XV.745-879]; Book XV · Fable VIII [XV.745-879], normalized characters 6525-7002
star.excerpt: Hardly had he uttered these words, when the genial Venus, perceived by none, stood in the very midst of the Senate-house, and snatched the soul, just liberated {from the body}, away from the limbs of her own Cæsar, and, not suffering it to dissolve in air, she bore it amid the stars of heaven. And as she bore it, she perceived it assume a {train of} light and become inflamed; and she dropped it from her bosom. Above the moon it takes its flight, and, as a star, it glitters

narrativeBlocks.title: Venus sees danger
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ovid's Book XV, Venus fears the plot against Julius Caesar and pleads with the gods. The passage frames Caesar as her descendant through Aeneas.

narrativeBlocks.title: A plea against the conspiracy

narrativeBlocks.title: A soul becomes a star
narrativeBlocks.body: After a divine speaker asks that Caesar's soul become a beam of light, Venus carries it from the Senate-house and the poem describes it among the stars.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read apotheosis as poetic reception
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid's episode is literary and politically situated praise. It is not eyewitness evidence for Caesar's death or proof that a literal transformation occurred.

narrativeBlocks.title: An ending with an audience
narrativeBlocks.body: The passage joins Venus's ancestry, Caesar's deification, and Augustus's public position in a poem that also turns toward Ovid's own hoped-for poetic survival.
